text: A wedding costs money that a Bronx taxi does not bring in, and that arithmetic drives everything else. Richard Brooks keeps the scale domestic: a kitchen, a hallway, the price of things said out loud. The plan swells past anything the occasion requires, and the further it swells the harder it gets for anyone in the family to say so. The comedy is in the guest list. The drama is in what the guest list stands for — a marriage run on questions nobody asked, a daughter turned into the pretext for an argument that is not about her, a husband who counts fares and is expected to absorb the total. Ninety-four minutes, no subplot to hide in, and inside single scenes the tone slides from funny to bleak and back. The National Board of Review put it among their ten for 1956.

Two fourteen-year-olds trail a concert pianist through Manhattan, and the pianist is the least interesting person in the arrangement. George Roy Hill puts the girls on foot: parks, staircases, side streets, entire afternoons spent shadowing a grown man who has done nothing to earn the attention. The crush is genuine and also a pretext — a game with rules only the two of them know, which gives the school year somewhere to go. Henry Orient himself is a comic figure whose dignity does not survive being observed, and the farce is extracted from him at length. The other register runs quieter. Friendship at that age has weather in it, and the film is arranged so that a shift in that weather lands harder than anything happening to the man they are following.

Only one man in the patrol knew where they were going, and a bullet from someone nobody saw removes him early. What is left is a sergeant, a compass bearing taken on faith, and Mesopotamian sand with nothing in it to steer by. John Ford had seventy-three minutes and gave himself almost nothing else to use: an oasis, a small group of soldiers, an enemy who stays off screen and fires from beyond the frame. The dread is procedural — water, the watch rotation, who sleeps and who stands up in the open. Every hour costs the group something, and the arrangements have to be made again with fewer hands. The score took an Academy Award, which makes sense of the design: when the opposition is never shown, music has to supply the pressure the image withholds.

The threat arrives as paperwork: keep the boy, or keep the life he has been raised in. Murray has no job and no plan to get one, and for a twelve-year-old nephew that has been an education — an apartment run on his uncle's terms, a schedule made of whims, a working demonstration that a man can decline the whole arrangement. Then child welfare opens a file and names a condition. Fred Coe keeps most of this in rooms and on New York pavements and lets the talk run long; the sentences are shaped the way stage sentences are, and the film is better for not disguising it. What sharpens everything is the boy's position. He wants the household to survive, he can see what surviving will cost, and the negotiating goes on over his head between adults who each believe they are on his side.

She arrives from Hong Kong with a marriage already arranged, to a nightclub owner who has been keeping company with one of his own singers. Henry Koster spends 133 minutes and a colour budget on the collision; the costumes took an Academy Award and they are doing visible work, since the film plays across two kinds of display — family rooms in San Francisco's Chinatown, and a club stage a few streets and one generation away. Which promises made elsewhere still bind here is the question sitting under the courtships. It behaves like the 1961 studio musical it is, numbers halting the plot dead and comic business filling the space between, and the interest lies in watching a form built for spectacle handle an argument about obligation. Two women, one man, and a genre that settles such things by singing.

One minute, one action, and in 1896 that was enough to fill a slot on a programme. There is no story: two people arrange themselves, exchange a few words the film cannot carry, and do what the title says. The interest is in the arithmetic. Film was finite, so whatever got spent on had to be something people would pay to see and then pay to see again, and what they paid for here was not a train or a parade but two adults being affectionate in front of a machine. The performers work at theatre pitch, since nothing had yet asked them for anything smaller, and the gestures are sized for a hall rather than a face. Sixty seconds of business, performed for no audience present and every audience afterwards. It is in the National Film Registry.

There is a man hiding in the barn, and the children who find him have been taught exactly one story that fits. A working Lancashire farm, adults with animals to see to and no attention left for what the young ones are doing in the outbuildings. Bryan Forbes plays the belief straight — no wink, no narrator sorting error from truth — and the logic holds, because a Sunday school vocabulary has an answer ready for a bleeding stranger who came from nowhere. So they begin bringing him things. Secrets this size do not stay with three children, and the circle widens into something resembling a congregation. What the man actually did stays offscreen, carried by the audience and not by them, and the distance between those two knowledges is the film. Ninety-nine minutes, and never once condescending to the children.

The names on the records are not the names of the people playing on them. A pool of Los Angeles session musicians turned up to dates for Frank Sinatra, the Beach Boys and Bing Crosby, played what the arrangement needed, took the fee and went home to hear the results on the radio with somebody else's face on the sleeve. Denny Tedesco's documentary is built from the two things this story has: the players talking, and the recordings, which settle every argument the talking raises. The strongest stretches are technical — a musician describing what he did on a take, then the take. Underneath sits an ordinary working life that happened to produce the sound of an era. It is in the National Film Registry, which is one way of finally getting the names written down.

Before the bombing they were four children in Birmingham, and Spike Lee spends a long time there before going anywhere near September 15, 1963. The interviews are with parents, siblings and classmates, people who have told this story many times and are asked once more to describe a child. That reversal is the method. The crime is famous and the four are not, so the running time goes to the four. Lee also sits down with George Wallace, long out of office, and keeps the camera on him past the point where watching is comfortable. Birmingham appears as a functioning city with ordinary streets and ordinary Sundays, which is harder to render than a symbol and does more damage. A hundred and two minutes, and it took the Academy Award for documentary feature.

Nobody aboard asks the man for a ticket, and one mistaken assumption later he is running the boat. The passengers take the stowaway for a Party cultural officer; he finds the role fits, and it takes very little time before the Vistula cruise has a programme of organised amusements that nobody wants and nobody feels able to skip. Sixty-five minutes, made in Poland in 1970, and not one line explains itself. It does not need to. The comedy is entirely in manner — the voice people find when addressing someone who might be official, the speed with which volunteers step forward, the gravity brought to judging a pointless contest. Marek Piwowski keeps everyone talking in the register of a committee meeting that has drifted onto water. Rejs is on the Najlepsze filmy polskie list.

Two tickets, one sleeping compartment, and a night between a Polish city and the Baltic coast. Jerzy Kawalerowicz builds the film out of that geometry: sliding doors, corridors the width of one person, windows giving onto other windows, no conversation that is not partly public. Marta has a discarded lover aboard who will not let her be, which keeps a private pressure running underneath. Then the police get on, looking for a murderer. A carriage of strangers who had been mildly curious about one another turns into a crowd that only needs pointing, and how fast the pointing happens is the thing to watch. 1959, ninety-seven minutes, and the menace in Pociąg is social rather than criminal — produced by people observing each other decide what to believe.

A theatre that floats has to keep moving, because the audience is only ever the next town along the river. That makes the show boat a business before it is a romance: a company living at close quarters, rehearsing between landings, dependent on whoever can be put in front of the curtain tonight. Tonight it is the captain's daughter, kept off the stage until now. Her mother knows the trade and what it costs, objects, is overruled — and the objection stays in the room rather than being laughed away by the girl's success. James Whale directs 113 minutes of it in 1936, songs performed as labour, to paying customers, by people whose next meal depends on the receipts. The National Film Registry has it.

An ankle turns in the wings, and the assistant stage manager who has spent the run handling other people's props is on. Ken Russell gives that anecdote 137 minutes, the first sign that the anecdote is not what he is after. The company is provincial, the revue is cheap, and a substitution like this reorders everybody: who watches from the side, who recalculates, who is generous and who only appears to be. The numbers take the running time. It is 1971 and the shabbiness of the theatre is not softened anywhere. The original song score took an Academy Award. The understudy, meanwhile, does the steps correctly and would rather not be noticed, which is the wrong instinct for the job and precisely the right one for the film built around her.

A dinosaur was easier to imagine in 1914 than to animate: every frame of her had to be drawn by hand, and twelve minutes is a great many frames. What Winsor McCay bought with that labour was not a trick but a temperament. Blackton and Cohl had made objects move and shapes transform; here is a creature that seems to want things, to hesitate, to respond, and wanting things is a different order of drawing. The method underneath was new as well: keyframe animation, motion planned in advance rather than a picture repeated with small changes. Twelve minutes, one character, one hand, and no shortcut available anywhere in it. It is in the National Film Registry.
